2cbd852b8af9873c: Sure, running emulated Game Boy games at 30 fps with four shades of gray on an E Ink screen is cool, but you know what's cooler? A custom open source E Ink driver that could theoretically let any display do the same thing. YouTuber Bo Made It published a video last week demonstrating what he calls the InkBoy on a tiny ESP32-S3-powered e-paper board. It looks just about as good as the old-fashioned olive-green screen on the original Game Boy, which isn’t saying much, but it’s an impressive feat to make this work on a cheap stock e-paper screen. For those who haven’t owned an e-reader, E Ink displays are great at what they’re designed for. They can retain what's on the screen without continuously consuming energy by using electrical pulses to move charged pigment particles within individual pixels, enabling them to store the screen state physically. That makes e-paper devices very power efficient, but it comes with a huge trade off: Changing those pixels is a glacially slow process compared with the modern displays we're all accustomed to. The screen that Bo used to make his InkBoy, for example, has a refresh speed of around 300 milliseconds, which is actually on the faster end of e-paper displays - but only really practical for displaying static images. Standard black and white E Ink displays contain two types of pigments: Positively charged black ones, and negatively charged white pigments. Swapping between the two requires a series of brief electrical charges in a particular waveform pattern that gradually move the pixels from the front of the screen to the back, clearing out most of the pigment that shouldn’t be at the surface. The native driver in Bo’s Waveshare 1.54-inch ESP32-S3 e-paper display does just that, and it doesn’t leave a lot of room for displaying motion. In order to get around those limitations, Bo built his own driver for the display that shortened the waveform and enabled per-pixel driving to reduce image ghosting. More impressively, it enabled his ostensibly black and white screen to display four shades of grey, just like an original Game Boy. He was originally using dithering to create greyscale images, but it honestly looked horrible. Luckily Bo noticed something while trying to fix the issue of image ghosting. “I noticed the display was already producing grey - just accidentally,” he said in his video. “The pigment doesn’t instantly jump from black to white, so I wondered if I deliberately stop driving it partway through the transition, can I produce those grey levels on demand?” The answer was yes, and with some additional tweaking he was able to produce those grey levels at 30 frames per second - a vast improvement from the 3.33 frames per second available with the original driver. It’s an impressive accomplishment, but is it a first? Not quite, but it’s still a new way of approaching faster E Ink refresh times. As Bo explains, he got his idea from another YouTuber who built their own E Ink Game Boy, albeit with some entirely custom hardware that allowed them to bypass typical E Ink screen design to create their own faster display. What Bo did was code his own driver for stock hardware, making this an impressive accomplishment in its own right, and one enterprising user could theoretically reproduce on their own if desired. After a month of work, and with the admitted use of some vibe coding for the driver, Bo has published a working version of his driver on GitHub, but with a hefty warning: Not only can forcing custom waveforms and higher refresh rates on E Ink screens cause permanent damage, but long-term panel life wasn’t evaluated as part of his experiment, either. If you’re going to try this, in other words, do so at your own risk, and maybe not on your modded Kindle - buy a cheap E Ink screen to break instead. ®

faafd83f249a0314: Smartphone shipments fell by at least a fifth in the third calendar quarter as the AI-driven memory crunch battered another consumer hardware market. Preliminary estimates from IDC and Omdia put the year-on-year decline at 22 percent and 20 percent respectively. Memory costs have surged by approximately 350 percent since last year, according to IDC, and are still rising. This continues to place substantial pressure on vendor margins, prompting them to hike price tags and scale back on devices at the value end of the market. IDC estimates that vendors shipped 255.3 million smartphones into distribution channels and warns that the downturn is far from over. "The sharp downturn the industry has been bracing for finally materialized in the third quarter this year. However, the worst is yet to come," said Nabila Popal, IDC's senior research director for worldwide devices. "Current indicators suggest that the market has not yet reached the bottom. While memory inflation is beginning to slow down, with a low double-digit sequential increase in Q3 compared to a 50 to 100 percent jump in prior quarters, costs remain elevated across other critical components as well, compounding the crunch." Omdia puts shipments at roughly 255 million, close to IDC's estimate despite the different annual decline. It says that the shrinking market has further polarized the competitive landscape, with Samsung and Apple now accounting for about 45 percent of global shipments, up approximately 8 percentage points from a year ago, while rising costs hit more price-sensitive segments particularly hard. Omdia still expects global smartphone shipments to fall 12 percent across 2026, followed by another 6 percent decline next year. It previously forecast that devices priced above $400 would prove more resilient and could record shipment growth. "We don't anticipate any relief to the current memory crisis before 2028 at the earliest as we expect there to remain a considerable gap between demand and supply. The first signs of improvement we're looking for is when the memory pricing will stabilize (basically stopping to grow), and we're still not there yet," Omdia principal analyst Runar Bjorhovde told The Register. Omdia says investment in distribution partnerships and premium devices could determine which vendors emerge stronger when costs ease. New flagship launches, promotions, and festive demand in Q4 are unlikely to fully offset persistent supply-side pressures. Omdia reckons buyers may get used to paying more, potentially creating greater opportunities for higher-value devices. The firm previously outlined the measures some phone makers are taking to offset the rising cost of memory parts, including switching to cheaper display panels, sensors, or radio frequency (RF) modules. IDC also sees little prospect of recovery before 2028 and expects a lasting shift toward higher costs. It says vendors that adapt their products and pricing will be best placed to gain market share. ®

On Sept 27, Umno president Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the party had collected RM9.25 million for the fund.
Ummi also referred to the Tabung Haji controversy and sought the panellists' views on corruption and political accountability.
Her questions have since attracted attention on social media platforms, including TikTok and Instagram, where clips of the exchange drew likes and shares.
Reactions were mixed, with some users praising her willingness to raise the issues with political leaders, while others expressed differing views.
She posed the questions during the third edition of iFUTURE, held from Oct 11 to 13, which carried the theme "Redefining Future Leaders Through Value-Based Leadership".

The summit brought together 1,231 student leaders from 20 Malaysian public universities and 30 international universities, including 406 international participants from 53 countries and 310 Johorean university students.

Organised by the Higher Education Ministry through the Department of Higher Education, the summit provided a platform for dialogue between student leaders and figures from government, industry and academia.

24fe24649531e0a8: LONDON: A woman who alleges British actor and comedian Russell Brand raped her more than 25 years ago told jurors on Thursday that she found him "frightening", angrily rejecting his lawyer's suggestions that they had had consensual sex.

Brand, once one of Britain's most high-profile broadcasters and the former husband of US singer Katy Perry, is on trial accused of three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old denies the allegations and told police after his arrest that he had never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity.
Prosecutors on Wednesday described him as a ruthless sexual predator as his career progressed from stand-up comedy to becoming a TV presenter and later a Hollywood movie star.
Woman says she did not think she would be believed
On the second day of his trial at London's Southwark Crown Court, a woman said Brand raped her in her room after meeting at a fringe event during the 1999 Labour Party conference.
"We were just there for him to abuse and consent was irrelevant," she told the jury.

Winter asked: "You didn't struggle, did you?" She replied: "I didn't struggle, no, I didn't. I couldn't struggle, I couldn't breathe".

Winter asked the woman why she did not report the alleged rape to the police at the time, to which she replied: "I was ashamed. I didn't think anybody would believe me, this is 1999."
'I didn't consent'

She told the jury that she felt guilty hearing about other allegations against Brand, becoming emotional as she said: "Had I come forward, would it have stopped?"
At the conclusion of her evidence, she said: "I can 100% tell you, on everything I hold dear, that I didn't consent."
Trial due to last six weeks
Brand is alleged to have tried to drag a woman into a toilet cubicle at MTV Europe where she worked in 2001 and separately to have orally raped a woman in a toilet cubicle in a bar in 2004.

He said the women whose allegations were featured in the documentary were not part of the trial and their accusations had not been tested in court.

He added: "The defence may suggest the programme caused the complainants, or at least some of them, to revisit historic sexual events and in their memories twist them from the consensual acts they were to the crimes they now allege".
The trial is expected to last around six weeks.

f8710d8cf6f902e4: Don't need a full-fat productivity suite and worried about where your documents are being stored? Welcome to TinyLittleOffice, a set of applications where the document is the link itself. Using a URL to stash information isn't new. Look at many URLs, and you'll see a lengthy sequence of seemingly random characters at the end. Using that space to stash data isn't novel, but using it for documents is an interesting approach. TinyLittleOffice comprises a selection of tools, including a basic word processor, presentation builder, spreadsheet, calendar, and a drawing tool. The theory is a simple one: create a document and get a link. The link is the document. The document isn't saved on a server or made into an attachment (although it is possible to export to a variety of formats), so it is, in theory, private. That is, unless you're worried about what the server is doing when it opens the link. Using the URL for documents is far from a completely new idea. Paul Ford's (the author) "co-conspirator," Rich Ziade, came up with the idea of TinySheet six years ago: a simple spreadsheet that ran in the browser and kept its data in the URL. "We moved on," wrote Ford, "and sadly, those sites fell off the web, and the old links all broke." Years later, the concept was resurrected and expanded to include other productivity tools. The server code is on GitHub, which should, in theory, at least ease concerns about the new links rotting away. We tested the project, and it is indeed very impressive from a technical standpoint. It can easily create short documents and spin up spreadsheets. Sure, it won't make LibreOffice lose any sleep, but it's a fun tool, and sending increasingly lengthy URLs (there is a URL shortener on tap, though they do expire) is a lightweight alternative to a document attachment. And there's the rub. Why not simply use a tool that creates a document? As Ford acknowledges, "There are lots of tradeoffs. This is not, in any way, how web apps are expected to work. The links can get unwieldy pasted in chat, and you can't upload video or images, full stop. It's not collaborative like Google Docs. It's collaborative like handing out zines at a street fair." However, to carp about what TinyLittleOffice doesn't do is to miss the point. It is lightweight by design – it has to be in order to cram document data into the link. Ford called it "disposable software," which is true. "Everything in tech is huge right now," writes Ford. "Every system lives on someone else’s machine and tracks you everywhere. All the content you make with those systems is being gobbled by LLMs. "Meanwhile, most normal people are in chat all day, hiding out from the mess, rambling about politics and sports on WhatsApp or coordinating mutual aid on Signal. "I really enjoyed building something for them/us." ®

24484194057efa41: JAKARTA: Indonesia has begun testing the use of dry ice to disperse thick haze caused by forest fires in South Sumatra, deploying 1,600kg in an experimental weather modification operation yesterday.

"Preliminary reports indicate an improvement in visibility around the seeding area, from approximately 650 metres to 2,800 metres," he said in a statement.
South Sumatra is among Indonesia's six priority provinces for forest and land fire suppression, alongside Riau, Jambi, West Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan and South Kalimantan.
Berton said the operation used a Cessna Caravan aircraft, which departed from Raden Inten II Airport in neighbouring Lampung province and dispersed dry ice at an altitude of about 4,500 feet.
He said the technique aimed to disrupt atmospheric conditions that trap thick smoke near the ground, allowing it to rise and disperse to improve visibility.
Unlike conventional weather modification, which uses sodium chloride to stimulate rainfall, the dry ice technique does not depend on the availability of rain clouds, he said.

The trial is scheduled to continue until Oct 18, after which the results will be evaluated and further discussions held with relevant parties on whether to expand the technique to other areas affected by forest and land fires.

9bc422dc42e404d3: PILGRIMS in Saudi Arabia may not have anticipated being caught up in an air war, but some experienced an attack by Yemen's Houthis first-hand and others have been forced to change their plans.

Footage of the blast that killed 13 people and wounded 300 in a Riyadh airport departure terminal struck on Saturday showed many passengers attired in the simple white clothes of Muslim pilgrims travelling to Makkah.
Saudi media reported that a Bangladeshi imam leading a group of dozens of pilgrims was killed and others wounded in the attack.

While the Houthis have promised not to attack Makkah and Madinah, the two holiest places in Islam that attract millions of pilgrims each year, they are targeting other Saudi airports in what they call retaliation for Saudi attacks on them.
"I feel deeply worried for my family and myself," said Fadi Anwar, a Jordanian living in Makkah.
"We constantly receive warnings (phone alerts from the authorities) and it causes us great anxiety."

Saudi officials have said the kingdom is safe and that the security of visitors is valued above all else, an offer of reassurance even as Western governments have warned against using most Saudi airports.

Although most international pilgrims fly directly into Madinah or Jeddah airports, many others travel via Saudi Arabia's other main air hubs, including the many pilgrims who already live in the kingdom.

Al Amin Hassan Mohammed from Sudan, who was visiting Saudi-based family members before a pilgrimage to Makkah, said he had been in Riyadh during Saturday's attack, which sent him and neighbours onto the street.
"We were tired and worried. We went out of the houses and we talked with each other," he said.

Mohammed, who has a married daughter in Saudi Arabia's city of Dammam, close to Dhahran where the Houthis targeted a Saudi Arabian Oil Company building on Tuesday, has made the pilgrimage to Makkah before.
The vast courtyard of the enormous main mosque in Makkah was a swirl of pilgrims in their white robes on Tuesday, as they circled the Kaabah, the point towards which all Muslims face to pray.
Makkah draws millions of people each year, both during haj and for umrah, from both inside Saudi Arabia and overseas, and the attacks have made some nervous.

The strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-allied Houthis, resulting from the reignition of Yemen's civil war as a spillover from the United States-Iran conflict, have caused Saudi Arabia to ground many flights.
Schools in Riyadh have been switched to online learning this week and some offices have told staff to work from home.

The disruption has been particularly acute for those trying to travel, a group that includes pilgrims, business figures attending Saudi Arabia's many high-profile conferences, Saudi tourists wishing to go on holiday and foreign residents wanting to fly home.
"We've had some trips postponed. We had friends who were travelling; it was delayed, they didn't travel," said Mohammed.
His friends had been planning to fly via Riyadh but in the end they took a boat back to Sudan from Jeddah, he said.
A senior executive Reuters spoke to on Wednesday was busy arranging transport for foreign employees, sending them by road to Doha in Qatar for onward flights.
A diplomat in Riyadh said several embassies had also used Doha for trips to and from Saudi Arabia over recent days, including for staff temporarily leaving with their families.
The representative of a company organising transport to Doha and Dubai said fares to those destinations had doubled.

Being prepared to pay is no guarantee of travel — in the early phases of the US-Iran war, Iranian fire grounded many flights around the Gulf and that direct conflict may erupt again with US President Donald Trump threatening to resume strikes.

2ec3dd1b51457014: MORE and more Malaysians now shop online rather than in brick-and-mortar shops, departmental stores and malls.
With the new trend, instances of consumers getting shortchanged or outright cheated via e-commerce platforms are also growing.
It is thus most welcome and timely that the government is finally acting with the drafting of the E-Commerce Bill, hopefully to be tabled in Parliament soon.

Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali has announced that among the key features in the proposed law is a proposal to introduce a licensing regime for e-commerce platform operators, including those based overseas but offering services to Malaysians.
This is a sensible requirement of accountability, as any business entity targeting our consumers ought to come within the ambit of Malaysian rules and regulations.

Consumer protection, above all, must keep pace with the growth of digital commerce. Buyers should not be exposed to unsafe products, misleading claims, fraudulent sellers or unresolved disputes simply because transactions take place online.
Online platforms cannot remain as mere intermediaries. Marketplaces that profit from facilitating transactions must shoulder appropriate responsibility for the sellers of products on their platforms.

Licensing must, therefore, establish clear obligations rather than become just a box-ticking exercise. Protections must be afforded not just to Malaysian consumers, but also to our own online platforms.

There should not be any double standards where foreign platforms are not subject to laws governing Malaysian platforms. It is already tough enough for these platforms and sellers to compete against foreign counterparts, given the latter's business scale that our own online businesses can only dream of.

Malaysian businesses should not have to compete against foreign entities that exploit regulatory gaps or evade obligations imposed on domestic traders. Our traders deserve, at the very least, a level playing field.
While licensing and other regulations governing businesses, online and otherwise, are inevitable, the government must also watch against over-regulation.

The high cost and difficulty of doing business are often related to bureaucratic delays caused by compliance requirements. Strong oversight may be a necessary fact of doing business, but the regulatory framework should avoid imposing disproportionate compliance costs on smaller businesses or make it harder for legitimate domestic entrepreneurs to reach online customers.

There is also a case for aligning our e-commerce laws with international models, not least so that if our platforms go global one day, they will not be hamstrung. As commerce increasingly navigates online, these reforms cannot come any sooner.
Done right, updating our rules for digital commerce will build public confidence in online shopping security while ensuring a fairer environment for both consumers and Malaysian businesses.

bfeeb5deaaa2b516: ONE message told him to "go to hell". Others said he deserved to be imprisoned. Death threats poured in.
Asians who share a name with one of the men accused of raping a United States university student have faced a torrent of online abuse.
The alleged 2024 gang rape of a Cornell University student, detailed in a recent suit, has sparked an outpouring of outrage against the seven accused perpetrators.
The case has sent Internet sleuths scouring digital footprints for clues to track them down.
One of the accused is a Korean man identified by US media as Winston Lee. The problem is that the world is full of people named Winston Lee.

The rage misdirected at people who share that name, some of whom live outside the US and look nothing like the accused, lays bare the perils of a chaotic Internet, where people distrustful of public institutions become digital detectives.

One of those wrongly identified was a Chinese American whose LinkedIn profile identifies him as a New York-based finance professional who graduated from Cornell University in 2020 — four years before the alleged rape.
"You can't hide. Your future is over," said one message he received via LinkedIn.
"You'll get exactly what you deserve... which is prison!! You'll be gang raped there."
Another said that a "black magic" spell had been cast upon him.
In a video on TikTok — where his bio reads "Not part of Cornell7" — he said he had hired a lawyer to press charges against a woman who posted his phone number and his parents' address online.
After a deluge of hateful messages, another man misidentified as Winston Lee posted a personal appeal to TikTok detectives.

"I am Indonesian and not the Winston Lee named in the recent Cornell University case. Please verify the identity of the person you are looking for before contacting, tagging, or making accusations against someone."
After a similar flood of messages, a Chinese-American student named Winston Lee at the University of Pennsylvania added a disclaimer to his LinkedIn profile: "I do not go to Cornell."
Those appeals did not appear to slow what Reddit discussion boards described as an "online hunt" for the seven accused, drawing many users down Internet rabbit holes.
With few verified details about the man actually accused, Internet users continued searching aggressively for his whereabouts.
One Reddit post claimed Winston Lee was now serving in the South Korean army. Another user on X said she had received tips suggesting he had been spotted on Cornell University's campus.
People with names like the other six accused also complained about rage spamming and threats.
"These social justice warriors are literally messaging and harassing the wrong" people, said podcast host Brad Polumbo.
"These things should be litigated through the criminal process or through some sort of fair process, not through a social media mob or witch hunt."
A group of former Cornell students, who belonged to the same Chi Phi fraternity as the seven accused but graduated before the alleged incident, also complained of online smear campaigns.

"They are being wrongfully accused on social media of having involvement, are consequently receiving death threats and related hate mail," their attorney Adam Ford wrote in a letter to the university that was obtained by AFP.
"Most of them have had their employers and higher education institutions take adverse actions against them, including being placed on leave."
Digital sleuths have for years misidentified accused perpetrators of high-profile shootings and other crimes, exposing them to abuse.

Such misidentification can further roil an already chaotic information ecosystem and hinder the actual investigation by generating false leads, warned Mike Rothschild, a researcher who studies conspiracy theories.

"The wrongfully accused are often hounded. They sometimes have to go into hiding, or get death threats, or are even violently attacked themselves. And there is no penalty for being wrong on the part of those accusing them."
The writer is from AFP

d699b1ef9bbd16e7: PETALING JAYA: PAS does not need to hold the opposition leader’s post, as the party has 43 MPs to advance its agenda in the lower house, Iskandar Abdul Samad said.

The PAS treasurer said although the opposition leader has traditionally been accorded more time on the floor, the number of MPs the Islamic party has allows them to address various issues and promote its stance.

Earlier today, former Umno Supreme Council member Puad Zarkashi, who quit Umno earlier this year, suggested that PAS take over the role of opposition leader from Hamzah Zainudin, who is Wawasan president.
“There is no need for PAS to pay him any attention,” Iskandar told FMT, referring to Puad.
“The party ignored him even when he was with Umno,” he added.
Puad, who is also the former Batu Pahat MP, described Hamzah as unimpressive during the debate on the 2027 budget.
He said Hamzah had failed to offer new proposals or policies in his budget debate, only mentioning the need for an “engine of high-impact economic growth”.
Hamzah has been opposition leader since December 2022 although he stepped down for a short period from April to June following his sacking by Bersatu.
PAS vice-president Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar, the Perikatan Nasional chairman, took over the role during that time before Hamzah returned as opposition leader in June.
931da2ccfa1b9d51: WASHINGTON: The firing squad execution of a convicted military base shooter will not be livestreamed, US president Donald Trump announced Thursday, cancelling a contentious plan by defense secretary Pete Hegseth.

The move to livestream Nidal Hasan's execution was widely opposed at home and abroad, prompting outrage from both US Democratic and Republican politicians, the Catholic Church, rights groups and the UN.
The cancellation is a blow to Hegseth, who is already under fire over the stalemated Iran war and its fallout, which are weighing on the Republican Party's chances in upcoming midterm elections.
Hasan "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

The US president indicated that he did not personally oppose the streaming plan, saying that it "might have been a strong deterrent for the world to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan".

But "many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die," Trump said, adding that the execution could still be viewed in person by immediate families of the victims if they wanted to do so.
Hasan's execution - scheduled for Dec 3 at Fort Hood, Texas, where he gunned down 13 people in 2009 - is set to be the first by a US military firing squad since 1945.
Hegseth said last week that "we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," later confirming that the plan was to livestream the execution.
506f94c283a2d476: KDE is marking its 30th birthday by showing X11 sessions the door. The newly released KDE Plasma 6.8 is Wayland-only, though X11 applications can still run through XWayland. The change arrives right on schedule after last month's beta. KWin handles both window management and display-server duties. That means X11-based screen-recording tools, for example, won't work any more. You can't "shade" windows – roll them up into the title bar and back – and that's not planned to come back. Restoring saved sessions can also behave differently. Applications cannot freely position their own windows under Wayland, leaving placement to the compositor. Saying that, there are lots of tweaks and refinements in this release. The Spectacle screenshot tool can now include system audio and microphone input in its screen recordings. Plasma 6.8 integrates with non-KDE tools better. For instance, KDE's browser integration now supports the Flatpak version of Microsoft's Edge browser. GTK2 applications also get better dark-theme matching. Internationalization is getting better – for example, the Clock understands the Bikram Sambat calendar, and Amharic is now supported in KDE's on-screen keyboard. The System Monitor app has better tracking of VRAM usage as well as main memory, and can pin tasks to certain CPU cores. There's better multi-monitor handling: screens are color-coded as well as by make and model, which is helpful if you have multiple identical monitors. There are more authentication options in KDE's VPN support too. The Union theming system is in beta, though not enabled by default. KWin can also apply matching effects to windows with client-side decorations, such as Valve's Steam client. Plasma's High Dynamic Range (HDR) support is better: it follows ICC color profiles, and understands Hybrid Log Gamma. On Nvidia GPUs, Plasma 6.8 enables triple-buffered output, resulting in smoother animations and transitions. Speaking of animations, more system effects – such as desktop "peek" and window "aperture" (when windows slide to the edge of the screen out of the way) – now respect the global animation settings. The Wayland-only session requires alternatives to remote-access tools that depend on an X11 desktop session, but the built-in Remote Desktop server, based on KRdp, has been improved. It's faster, it can adapt to slower connections on the fly, the clipboard is now bi-directional between host and remote system, and an exclusive mode can lock the host's screen while providing a virtual display sized to the client's window. KRdp uses Microsoft's Remote Desktop Protocol, but there's also Krfb if you prefer VNC instead. If you really need individual remote Wayland applications over SSH, then Waypipe is the way to go. The full changelog has all the details of the changes. Kubuntu 27.04 – recently announced as being codenamed "Tenacious T-Rex" – should include Plasma 6.8 when it arrives in April next year. KDE's internal metrics showed more than 95 percent of Plasma 6.6 users running Wayland in June. Including older versions, adoption was about 76 percent. Even so, we suspect that some users won't be happy with this change. With 6.8 out of the door, and on its way into fast-moving distros near you, the SonicDE project, which aims to continue development of the X11-capable KWin from Plasma 6.7, may start to pick up more interest. The KDE Project started with founder Matthias Ettrich's announcement on the de.comp.os.linux newsgroup on October 14, 1996. Before KDE, there were some commercial proprietary Unix desktop environments that were ported to Linux. For instance, Caldera OpenLinux 1.0 shipped with Visix's Looking Glass – you can see a tiny screenshot of it in the OpenLinux 1.1 announcement – but none ever went FOSS. Xfce is slightly older – as founder Olivier Fourdan described in this 2009 article: "I started the project in late 1996, before GNOME or gtk+ even existed." The XForms Common Environment was released first, but in those early days, what was then called XFce wasn't open source. It also started out as a recreation of CDE, which was finally open sourced in 2012. This makes it an early equivalent of NsCDE, which we compared with the real thing in 2022. In its early days, the Qt C++ toolkit that KDE chose caused problems, which led to the establishment of the KDE Free Qt Foundation in case something bad happened to its creators. Qt's licensing situation improved in 2000, when Qt 2.2 became available under both the GPL and QPL, resolving the GPL-compatibility concerns surrounding KDE's foundations. Even holdout Red Hat started bundling KDE. Thirty years on, KDE remains one of the great survivors of the free desktop. Long may it continue. ®
6388b3d480b1995c: Genuine human creativity takes time, but you know what doesn't? AI slop. There are countless AI models out there that can make something that passes for music, and you might come across those tracks on streaming services without realizing it. Google says it will begin labeling that content in YouTube Music, building on similar disclosures in the main YouTube app.
Google is not outright banning AI music or even speaking ill of it. "Generative AI is opening up new ways for artists to create, experiment, and share music," the company says in a blog post.

ea0bee2c7a155f39: Coral-fringed tropical atolls are among the landforms most threatened by global warming, but many have a potential superpower: Healthy ecosystems may help them keep pace with rising seas.

Atoll islands with native vegetation and thriving seabird populations are “naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” said Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom, who led an international team of scientists that studied island resilience across 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans.

Their paper, published Wednesday in Science Advances, shows that restoring atoll ecosystems reinforces their growth. Seabirds ferry nutrients from the open ocean and deposit them on the atolls as guano that nurtures land plants, marine life and coral growth. This provides more material for reef building, as parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand to maintain beaches, while native plants with extensive root networks stabilize sediments.
f9edcbc85f7f676a: KUALA LUMPUR: A total of 13,743.15 tonnes of battery waste classified under scheduled waste code SW103 were generated nationwide between 2021 and 2025, according to the Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Ministry (NRES).
The ministry said the figure covered all battery waste under the code and was not limited to electric vehicle (EV) batteries.
In a written parliamentary reply, NRES said seven off-site recovery facilities handling SW103 waste were operating in Kedah, Selangor, Johor, Perak, Negri Sembilan and Penang as of March 4.
"These facilities support the recovery of valuable materials from used batteries, including lithium, nickel and cobalt," the ministry said.
The ministry was responding to Mohd Nazri Abu Hassan (PN-Merbok), who asked about the number of EV batteries disposed of or recycled between 2021 and 2026.

He also asked whether the government planned to implement the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) principle, which would require EV manufacturers and importers to take back batteries and bear the cost of managing them at the end of their service life.

NRES said the government had outlined a direction for implementing EPR through the Circular Economy Policy Framework for the Malaysian Manufacturing Sector, led by the Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry (Miti).
The framework aims to extend manufacturers' responsibilities for managing products at the end of their life cycle, including through collection, reuse, remanufacturing and recycling.
However, a mandatory EPR mechanism requiring EV manufacturers and importers to take back used batteries and bear the cost of managing them had yet to be established, the ministry said.
It added that further study was needed on legal requirements, manufacturers' and importers' responsibilities, funding mechanisms and policy coordination between NRES and Miti.

The ministry said EV batteries classified as scheduled waste were regulated under the Environmental Quality Act and the Environmental Quality (Scheduled Wastes) Regulations 2005, specifically under code SW103.
Those generating battery waste are responsible for ensuring it is properly handled and stored, and sent to authorised premises in accordance with legal requirements.

4503713ba514f346: When a million veterans shared their genetic data by enrolling in the Department of Veterans Affairs' “Million Veteran Program,” they expected nothing back. This did not surprise Ravi Madduri, a senior scientist with the Data Science and Learning Division at the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Argonne National Laboratory. He is abundantly clear about the terms under which these veterans donated their data: “Even after giving everything to the country, they found it in their hearts to give more without expecting anything in return.” That gift, which constituted the nation’s largest biorepository and most ancestrally varied cohorts of veteran data in the world, created a debt that Madduri, who also holds a joint appointment in the Department of Human Genetics at the University of Chicago, is working to repay. “What I feel when I look at that data is that I have an obligation to deliver to the veterans on their intentions in doing this,” he says. Those intentions, as he reads it, are that others, veteran or not, can benefit from whatever the data can reveal. “We cannot dilly dally,” Madduri says. After arriving at Argonne as a graduate student in 2001, Madduri has spent the last two decades at the intersection of supercomputing and biomedicine, much of the time building the computing that turns the veterans’ data into results impacting areas from post-traumatic stress disorder to heart disease to cancer. He explains that machines have largely held up their end, but the obstacles between precious data and delivered results are not always solved with faster machines. Understanding the challenges is the path toward better science. What the Math Was Unable to Solve Any two human genomes differ at millions of specific positions. A genome-wide association study asks a seemingly simple question across an enormous volume of data. For example, does a given genetic variant travel together with a particular medical condition? On its own, the question is simple. Multiplied across every variant worth testing and every condition recorded in a patient's chart, it becomes an enormous math problem, which is what supercomputers exist to solve. The harder question is whether the code is written to let them. Madduri's team has run this problem on the Summit system at DOE's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility and on the Aurora system at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. On Summit, the team found that the job would not finish on the machine's CPUs. As the cohort grew, the matrix the analysis needed for each group no longer fit in memory, and the job stalled. “We decided to open the box and look at the code,” Madduri said. They found that the issue was not merely a speed problem, but a coding one. The analysis had been written for ordinary processors because that is what the genetics community was running on. Underneath the algorithms, though, the code spent nearly all of its time doing one thing: multiplying very large grids of numbers. This is exactly the operation that graphics processors exist to perform, and what makes them the engine of modern artificial intelligence training. As Madduri notes, the same computational architecture accelerating AI discovery “is also foundational for population genomics.” So, the team, led on this effort by Argonne's Alex Rodriguez, rewrote that part of the code for GPUs, and an analysis that would have taken roughly 481,000 CPU-core hours in the original version became tractable. This shift did more than speed up a slow job. It made a virtually impossible job possible. The workhorse they accelerated is a widely used genetics package called SAIGE, which made the rewritten version SAIGE-GPU, described in a separate paper in Bioinformatics. "We are not good at coming up with names. Sorry," Madduri says sheepishly. Before SAIGE-GPU, nearly every genome-wide association study started by picking a disease then looking for the variants linked to it. Madduri is blunt about the cost of that approach. “One of the challenges I found in biomedical research is that it is very incremental,” he explains. “Every year, they get new datasets, they analyze the data, they find a new set of genetic variants, and this happens across all of the different diseases.” The reason, he adds, is limited access to large-scale computing. His team chose not to be incremental and decided to solve the computational challenge once and for all. “One of the challenges we set for ourselves was to just take all the data that we have available, all the genetic data for all the veterans that have been sequenced as part of the Million Veteran Program,” Madduri says. The team, the Million Veteran Program consortium, published the results in Science, with Madduri's group among the authors, and published the computational work separately in Bioinformatics. The study reported on 2,068 traits across 635,969 veterans, and the results flagged 13,672 regions of the genome linked to one or more conditions. About 1,600 of these regions surfaced only because nearly a third of the participants were not of European ancestry. According to the Science paper, most genetic studies to this point have been drawn overwhelmingly from people of European descent. These 1,600 associations were previously “invisible” in the populations studied. That ancestral range also shaped how the analysis had to be run. The groups could not simply be pooled. That is, if a condition is more common in one ancestral group than another, the analysis has no way to tell a genuine disease marker from a marker of simply belonging to that group. Each group had to be run separately, and the results combined afterward. The 1,600 associations exist in no single group's results. They appear only when the separate analyses are combined. Madduri is careful about what the whole exercise means and what it does not. “This is all preclinical,” he says. “This is the discovery phase.” The analysis produces a statistical map of where to look. Turning any one of those 13,672 regions into a treatment takes years of downstream work by researchers who pick up and follow the data, which is why Madduri says the team never stopped. “Things that took 14 days when we wrote the Science paper now take less than a couple of hours,” he says. While this means getting an answer sooner, the real win is being able to ask the same question of a bigger population “with a larger cohort size and more statistical rigor than the paper that we published a couple of years ago.” When Data Cannot Travel The veterans’ genomes have an unusual advantage over other medical data. One agency gathered the data under one agreement, which is what made bringing them to Summit possible. In medicine, Madduri says, data “cannot be shared with one another as freely as you would probably share cosmology data.” The alternative is to move the model, he says: “Federated learning allows you to train models without moving data around.” This means each institution trains on the copy it already holds, behind its own walls, and only sends back the adjustments the model learned. Those adjustments are combined into a single updated model, which goes out to everyone, and the cycle repeats. Asked how several institutions are persuaded to compute together without pooling anything, he corrects the premise. “It is not the institution,” he says. “The first layer of that puzzle is people wanting to work together, to collaborate.” Then, the part that makes it work: “It is a people federation.” Madduri was a co-developer of APPFL, the Argonne Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning framework, which provides a means to help “move” models rather than data. The machinery underneath is closer to access control than to machine learning. "You do not have to write code for each scheduler," he says. Globus Compute presents one interface across the facilities' schedulers, and APPFL submits its training jobs through it. Even with these technical challenges, the harder problem is permission. “All the computing that happens is authorized computing that is tied to a project allocation,” Madduri says. Federated training means that each collaborator’s job has to run under their own institutional credentials on a machine they are personally entitled to use. A site with data nobody else has makes that shared model better for everyone. "If one site has data that are unique to it and other sites do not have that, then the model becomes more robust," Madduri adds. Many Different Worlds Madduri has been a regular attendee at the SC Conference since SC01 in Denver, which was themed “Beyond Boundaries,” and focused on moving data across them. “I was a grad student, and I had a demo in the DOE booth demonstrating my master’s thesis, which at that time was to use the Internet to move large amounts of data reliably from one point to the other,” he says. That capability was called reliable file transfer, and, in his words, it “has now transformed into what is called ‘Globus’.” The first tool he helped build moved research data around. The latest one lets the data stay in place. Since SC01, Madduri has been to the conference roughly 20 times and is specific about what he takes home. “I learn parallel processing, how people are scaling AI training, how people are dealing with parallelization, how people are dealing with resource utilization monitoring,” he notes. His group attends the Computational Approaches for Cancer Workshop every year. Lately, the interest has moved to AI agents. “The agentic approaches are the next frontier for us,” he declares. Madduri is also aware that he walks in unusual research domains. Before biomedicine, he worked with high-energy physicists, earthquake engineers, and cosmologists. “When I go to SC, I live in many different worlds,” he says. “I am part of a very small group of people that go to a [combined] human genetics conference and a supercomputing conference.” What Is Still Missing For Madduri, his debt is not settled. More than a decade after the first veterans enrolled, the Million Veteran Program data have produced a map but not yet a cure. What stands between those two things is the work of getting separate institutions to compute as one. To date, that still is being done largely by hand. “For the earlier experiments, it was us talking to NERSC, us talking to Argonne, us talking to Oak Ridge,” Madduri says. “It is a lot of human in the loop.” He is hoping the American Science Cloud being built under the DOE’s Genesis Mission will take that over: “It would be automated, run using APIs.” For now, Madduri remains focused on turning data into triumph, using a very special cohort of data to reveal the next breakthrough against cancer or spare someone a lifetime of anxiety. Until then, he marks progress one good idea, one technical advancement, and one SC Conference at a time. “My connection to Supercomputing, to SC, is long and very fruitful,” Madduri says. “I will be back in November, in Chicago, for SC26.” Join the Conversation at SC26 SC26 brings together the people building the computing infrastructure the work described herein depends on: systems, data platforms, networks, and storage that let research run at scale and across institutions. Attendees engage with technical papers, workshops, tutorials, posters, and Birds of a Feather (BoF) sessions covering AI, quantum computing, and HPC alongside practitioners from national laboratories, industry, and academia working on similar problems. Madduri will also be part of the SC26 Regional Tech Hub, a multimedia forum making its conference debut in Chicago, where he will contribute to the High-throughput Computing Infrastructures and Systems area. Join us in Chicago, November 15–20, 2026, for a week of discovery, collaboration, and community with a spotlight on regional technology leaders. Register today! Supplied by SC26
40c8cb9e6f6b153f: BANGKOK: The US wants its global partners to rename artificial intelligence (AI) as "super intelligence (SI)," convinced that the new moniker better reflects the emerging technology, a top US Treasury official told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.

Treasury undersecretary for international affairs Erin Browne said Washington was in negotiations with other shareholders of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about using the new term in a statement being drafted by the fund's steering committee, the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC).
US president Donald Trump last month directed US government agencies to use the words "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" when ​referring to the technology.
Browne said the US, which holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, wanted the change to take hold internationally as well.

"President Trump has been really clear on this, and he's, you know, using the term SI, and I think it's a clear priority for the US to use that term, and we think that more appropriately encapsulates the technology at hand," Browne said.
She declined to comment on whether Washington would refuse to sign off on the statement unless the switch was made.
"We're still in the middle of negotiations on that statement, so I'm not going to, you know, sort of run ahead of that," she said.
A source familiar with the matter said US officials had suggested during meetings on the IMFC statement that they would insist on the new language, raising eyebrows among some other IMFC members.

If Washington withholds its support for a consensus statement, the current IMFC chair, Saudi finance minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, could still issue a so-called chair's statement summarising the views of the members.
One possibility might involve skipping a mention of SI or AI and focusing on "new technology" instead, the source said.
The IMFC will hold a news conference and release any agreed statement led by Al-Jadaan and IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday.
"We see this as a driving force behind American growth and global growth," Browne said.

"Many countries are looking to the US to set the standards, as well as to set the path forward for SI development and how that can really enhance and boost growth and productivity on a global basis," Browne added.
76d2954e6354a26d: WHAT began more than a decade ago as a modest charitable initiative has grown into one of Bermaz Motor's most significant annual traditions: its annual golf tournament raises support for medical relief and vulnerable communities.

A golf course became a gathering point for philanthropy as Bermaz Motor brought corporate partners, government representatives and Mazda customers together for its 12th annual Mazda Charity Golf Tournament.
This reinforces the company's long-running effort to channel private-sector support to Malaysians in need.

Held on Oct 9-10 at Glenmarie Golf & Country Club, the event drew about 200 participants and raised support for the Mazda Medicare Fund (MMF), which provides medical assistance and humanitarian aid to underprivileged communities.
The charity luncheon on Oct 10 was graced by the Sultan of Pahang, Al-Sultan Abdullah Ri'ayatuddin Al-Mustafa Billah Shah, who has served as the fund's royal patron since 2015.

Also present were Health director-general Datuk Dr Mahathar Abdul Wahab, Pahang executive council member Datuk Mohamad Nizar Mohamad Najib and Malaysian Investment Development Authority chief executive officer Datuk Sikh Shamsul Ibrahim Sikh Abdul Majid.
Bermaz Auto Bhd executive chairman Tan Sri Ben Yeoh said the tournament had grown beyond a sporting event into a collective effort to support communities requiring assistance.
"Corporate responsibility must be lived, not stated," he said, adding that the event brought together industry players, public agencies, partners and customers around a shared purpose.

This year's beneficiaries include Mount Miriam Cancer Hospital, Pertubuhan Kebajikan Kanak-Kanak Yatim dan Cacat Perlindungan Selangor, Pusat Jagaan Anak-Anak Yatim Sai Pandian, Pertubuhan Rumah Anak Yatim dan Asnaf Kampung Sijangkang and Yayasan Al-Sultan Abdullah.
The organisations provide services spanning cancer care, welfare assistance and protection for orphans and vulnerable groups. Their representatives received symbolic mock cheques at the luncheon.

Established in 2015 through a collaboration between Prima Merdu Sdn Bhd and B. Braun Avitum Renal Services, the MMF initially focused on subsidised haemodialysis for financially disadvantaged patients with end-stage renal disease.
Its support has since extended to elderly care homes, orphanages, disability centres and facilities for children with special needs.
The fund said beneficiaries are assessed to ensure contributions are directed towards meaningful assistance, with donations allocated to charitable purposes rather than unnecessary overheads.
Bermaz Motor has also sought to sustain funding beyond the annual tournament through its Mazda Privilege Card, introduced in 2018.
The card carries a one-time RM100 registration fee that goes directly to the MMF and is eligible for tax exemption, subject to the applicable requirements.
Members also receive a 15 per cent discount on selected genuine Mazda spare parts and a 5 per cent discount on labour charges at Bermaz Motor and Prima Merdu Mazda service centres nationwide.
The programme gives Mazda owners another avenue to contribute to community support while accessing selected ownership benefits.

386dbd46d1012fc3: JERUSALEM: Israeli opposition politician Gadi Eisenkot, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival in upcoming elections, vowed Thursday to end Hamas rule in Gaza if he wins office following the Oct 27 vote.

"Today I give a public commitment: from the moment I enter the prime minister's office, within 18 months Hamas will no longer rule the Gaza Strip," the leader of the centre-right Yashar party said at a press conference near the war-ravaged Palestinian territory.

He said he would achieve this either by implementing US president Donald Trump's ceasefire plan, which provides for the gradual disarmament of Hamas and a transfer of power, or through "creative operations" by Israel's military aimed at destroying the Palestinian movement's military wing.

Hamas announced in July that it was disbanding its governing body to facilitate the transfer of Gaza's administration to a nascent technocratic Palestinian committee called the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
The NCAG, currently based in Cairo, was created following the declaration of a ceasefire last October and is overseen by Trump's Board of Peace.
Later in July, Hamas announced it had agreed to a deal involving the handing over of its weapons to the NCAG.
However, Israel has been sceptical, with Netanyahu demanding verifiable decommissioning of all weapons before any withdrawal of the military takes place.
Hamas has not gone ahead with disarmament, Israel has refused to reciprocate by starting to withdraw forces, and the NCAG is not operating inside the territory.
Israeli forces were allowed to stay in 53% of Gaza under the terms of the ceasefire, but a year later they control about 70%, according to official accounts.
Eisenkot's campaign pledge on Thursday is one of the strongest yet from the 66-year-old former military chief.
The close-fought election will be the first since Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which resulted in the deaths of more than 1,200 people.

In response to the attack, Israel launched a massive offensive in Gaza that has killed more than 74,300 people, according to the territory's health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are generally considered reliable by the UN.
Eisenkot on Thursday accused Netanyahu of a "strategic failure" in Gaza, where he said "Hamas is still the sovereign... armed, arming itself, and militarily active" after three years of war.
He also reiterated a pledge to establish a state commission of inquiry to identify those responsible for any security lapses leading up to Oct 7, a push the government has so far resisted.
"There is a way to prevent the next disaster," he said.

Eisenkot, like other opposition politicians, regularly accuses Netanyahu of bearing personal responsibility for the Oct 7 attack, notably by ignoring warnings from his security services and the UAE, according to media reports.
Netanyahu has categorically rejected the accusations and maintains that security officials did not wake him on the morning of the attack.
Current polls show that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor that led by Eisenkot is in a position to win the 61 seats needed to control the 120-seat parliament and form a governing coalition.
e8b47a2ddbdd5723: PETALING JAYA: Seorang pemimpin PAS berkata tidak penting bagi partinya untuk memegang jawatan ketua pembangkang kerana sudah mempunyai ruang mencukupi untuk menyuarakan pendirian menerusi 43 Ahli Parlimen.

bf45f35b1872b155: KUALA LUMPUR: Low Zi Yu continued her remarkable run at the World Junior Championships after securing a third consecutive girls' doubles medal, this time alongside Genevie Lim in Cairo today.
The second seeds lived up to their billing by sweeping aside Hong Kong's fifth seeds Au-Yeung Wing Chi-Chu Wing Chi 15-7, 15-7 in the quarter-finals to guarantee Malaysia at least a bronze medal.

Zi Yu, however, quickly picked herself up alongside Genevie to remain in the hunt for the elusive world junior gold.
She was girls' doubles runner-up with Dania Sofea Zaidi in 2024 before taking silver again alongside Noraqilah Maisarah Ramdan last year.
Genevie-Zi Yu, who were also bronze medallists at the Asian Junior Championships earlier this year, will next face China's 15th seeds Shi Si Chen-Xiang Yu Jin for a place in the final.
Malaysia narrowly missed out on another medal in the boys' doubles.

In mixed doubles, Irfan M Shazmir-Genevie came agonisingly close to joining the medal winners before China's Feng Yi Lang-Li Meng Han prevailed 15-8, 13-15, 16-14.
Malaysia's hopes of reaching Saturday's finals now rest on Genevie-Zi Yu, who will look to turn another guaranteed medal into a brighter colour.

34a78f915e58ada5: KUALA LUMPUR: Issues related to education, including aspects of student discipline and safety, teaching quality and the empowerment of skills education, took centre stage at the conclusion of the first week of the policy-level debate on the Supply Bill 2027 in the Dewan Rakyat.

Lim Guan Eng (PH-Bagan) suggested caning be reinstated in schools as one of the measures to address discipline and bullying issues, along with regular psychological evaluations for teachers assigned to carry out the punishment.

"Why was it that back in our school days in the 1970s – a time when caning was widely permitted – there were no cases of murder or rape like those we see today? In fact, there were no negative psychological effects on the students; many of them went on to become successful and prominent individuals," he said.

He also recommended emergency provisions for the installation of closed-circuit television cameras in more than 10,000 government schools nationwide, in addition to the establishment of a comprehensive anti-bullying and anti-sexual harassment support system, including increasing security patrols and engagement programmes with students and parents.

In agreement with Lim, Ramkarpal Singh (PH-Bukit Gelugor) emphasised that the issue of safety and bullying in schools should not be taken lightly and proposed a special allocation to train teachers to identify early signs of emotional stress and potential violence among students.
He also urged that each school be equipped with a sufficient number of counsellors and structured psychological assessment programmes to enable early intervention.

Issues related to education were also raised by several other MPs, including Ikmal Hisham Abdul Aziz (PN-Tanah Merah), William Leong (PH-Selayang) and Onn Abu Bakar (PH-Batu Pahat), who among other things urged that Form Six education be strengthened as an academic pathway to university and not considered as a last resort.

Touching on skills education, Richard Rapu (GPS-Betong) urged the government to expand access to technical and vocational education and training (TVET) for rural youth, especially in Sarawak, with training programmes aligned to the actual needs of the industry and job market.

"This skills training opportunity should not be concentrated only in big cities. Young people in rural areas and in Sarawak must also be given equal opportunities to learn and obtain better jobs," he said.

Muslimin Yahaya (PN-Sungai Besar) also agreed that TVET should be expanded to rural areas to provide opportunities for more than 50,000 students who are unable to obtain the Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia certificate each year due to failing in the Bahasa Melayu and History subjects.

Ali Biju (PN-Saratok) urged the education ministry to expedite the development of educational infrastructure in rural Sarawak to ensure that safe and quality learning facilities can be enjoyed by students, especially in remote areas.

Taking the example of the delay in the full replacement project of Sekolah Kebangsaan Abang Leman in Kabong, he said that stricter action should be taken against contractors who failed to meet the project schedules.
b907ca75934bc4fe: The online advertising industry has found a new way to make itself even more unpopular, with one adtech outfit accused of helping spyware vendors infect people's phones without them even clicking an ad. Researchers at Citizen Lab say they've uncovered the first publicly confirmed case of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack being delivered through targeted online ads, with devices at Al Jazeera among those infected. The technique, dubbed "AdFection," turns advertising networks into a spyware delivery system. Simply opening a website or app can be enough to trigger the attack, with no suspicious links or downloads involved. Israeli adtech firm Discover-Tech is allegedly behind the operation, according to researchers at Citizen Lab, which says the company acts as a middleman between the online advertising industry and multiple spyware and hacking vendors. "We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse," the researchers wrote. “In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose." Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform exploits the real-time bidding system that decides which ads appear on websites and apps. Every time someone loads a page, advertisers compete for available ad space and, in the process, receive information about the user's device and location. Discover-Tech allegedly used that data to identify specific targets and serve them malicious ads. One spyware vendor linked to the operation is Candiru, the Israeli developer now known as Integrity Labs. Citizen Lab traced attacks against at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025 to Candiru spyware delivered through ads from Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech didn't have to sneak into the advertising system, as Google and IAB Europe had listed the company as an approved vendor since 2020, apparently unaware of what it was Citizen Lab claims it was doing with that access. Citizen Lab sifted through nearly four billion ad-bidding records and found Discover-Tech ads on more than 70,000 mobile apps and 120,000 websites between March and June 2026. Some reached networks belonging to government agencies, defense organizations, and NATO. Researchers found no evidence that those organizations were infected, but they say the ads could have been used to profile devices on those networks. The researchers said the operation also covertly directed millions of devices toward servers associated with Candiru, although those connections don't necessarily indicate spyware infections. Google has since terminated Discover-Tech's access to its advertising exchanges and removed it from its approved vendor lists. IAB Europe followed suit, while Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi also took action. Discover-Tech and Candiru did not respond to Citizen Lab's requests for comment, nor ours. The researchers argue that the findings expose serious failings in an advertising industry that allowed a company with links to commercial surveillance operators to operate inside its supposedly vetted ecosystem for years. “Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report,” Citizen Lab said. For years, the worst thing about targeted advertising was that it knew far too much about you. Turns out some advertisers were interested in much more than your shopping habits. ®
09f546c7b9db62fc: BEIJING: Malaysia welcomes China's proposals to expand technology and knowledge transfer, as both countries seek to deepen strategic cooperation beyond conventional investment arrangements.

635209c73d3bc36a: BEIJING: China has reaffirmed its support for Malaysia's bid to become a full member of BRICS and expressed hope that the country will continue playing an important role in strengthening cooperation between China and Asean member states.

Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the support was reiterated during his meeting with Chinese Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang at the Great Hall of the People here today, following a similar assurances previously given by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
"Although President Xi had expressed his support earlier, China once again reaffirmed its backing for Malaysia's admission as a full BRICS member during today's discussions.

"China's support is important as the prime minister has already secured the agreement of the original BRICS member countries to back Malaysia's admission as a full member of the grouping," he told reporters after the meeting.
Zahid said China also hoped Malaysia would continue serving as a bridge in strengthening cooperation between China and Asean countries.
He said this included efforts to sustain trilateral cooperation among Asean, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and China through summits involving the three parties.
He said Malaysia had hosted the Asean-GCC-China Summit during the Asean Summit last year.
He said Malaysia was expected to continue playing a similar role when the next trilateral summit is held in China.
The cooperation also included efforts to promote the use of the renminbi in trade transactions with China and GCC countries.
Zahid said the move could also influence currency exchange arrangements involving the ringgit, renminbi and currencies of GCC countries.
China will assume BRICS chairmanship in 2027 and host the grouping's 19th Summit next year.
BRICS is an intergovernmental organisation established in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, with South Africa joining in 2011. — BERNAMA

d6e054a80ae7c297: TEHRAN: Iran's military on Thursday said an oil tanker had caught fire in the Gulf of Oman as it was attempting to pass through an area deemed prohibited, according to state television.
"A few hours ago... surveillance teams of the army's navy identified a non-compliant oil tanker that had caught fire," state television cited a military statement as saying.
"The offending tanker had switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through the prohibited zone," it added.
It was not immediately clear what caused the fire or who was responsible.
US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region and is enforcing a blockade on Iranian ports, did not immediately comment.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards announced the boundaries of the prohibited zone in September, after security chief Mohsen Rezaei proposed the measure.

In an interview with state television at the time, Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi said the zone would cover "part of the Sea of Oman and another part of the Arabian Sea, along the route that can lead to the Strait of Hormuz".
Tehran had said non-compliant vessels in the zone would face sanctions, without explicitly threatening military action against them.

Iranian naval forces have repeatedly targeted vessels they accused of using unauthorised routes through the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has declared closed since the outbreak of war with the US in February.
b09add531601b8be: JASIN: Police have crippled a drug distribution operation worth RM6.8 million, run single-handedly by a 27-year-old swimming coach.
The suspect was detained around 11.30am yesterday during a roadblock at the Lipat Kajang Toll Plaza, after police became suspicious of his Toyota Vios which was travelling from Johor.
Jasin police chief Superintendent Lee Robert said an inspection of the vehicle uncovered 3.70g of ketamine and 27.50kg of MDMA concealed in boxed-drink packets.

"Further investigations led to a follow-up raid at a condominium unit in Crescent Bay Suites, Johor Baru, at 4.50am today. The unit had been used as a drug storage facility and repackaging laboratory.

"An inspection of the unit led to the seizure of various drugs, including 17.8kg of MDMA, 29g of liquid and powdered ketamine, 21.60g of Erimin 5 pills and 32.2g of ecstasy pills," he said at a press conference at the Jasin police headquarters.
Lee said the suspect, who is from Johor, repackaged the drugs himself in juice packets before distributing them to entertainment outlets at prices ranging from RM300 to RM600 per packet.
"The total value of the drugs seized in both raids is estimated at RM6.808 million. Police also seized various equipment believed to have been used in the drug packaging operation," he said.
He said a urine screening test found the suspect positive for ketamine, adding that he had been involved in the activity since early this year.
The suspect has been remanded for seven days until Oct 21 to facilitate investigations into drug trafficking and self-administration under the Dangerous Drugs Act.
Lee said police were tracing other members of the distribution network and identifying the source of the drug supply.
c571066f6529308b: PUTRAJAYA: The Court of Appeal today upheld the High Court's dismissal of a suit filed by 21 contractors against the Attorney-General, the Chief Commissioner of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) and three others over claims of wrongful detention and malicious prosecution.
A three-member bench comprising judges Datuk Dr Choo Kah Sing, Datin Paduka Evrol Mariette Peters and Datuk Nadzarin Wok Nordin ruled that the appellants' appeal was without merit and dismissed it.

Delivering the court's decision, Choo said the appellants' complaint that they were forcibly imprisoned from Nov 16, 2014, to Nov 17, 2014, and that they were not detained in a place which has been gazetted for detention under the law is misplaced.

"With regard to the complaint of malicious prosecution, this court finds the mere fact that the appellants were found to be not liable at the close of the prosecution case in the Sessions Court, that could not equate to malicious prosecution.
"Weak evidence of poor prosecution is not malicious prosecution," he said.

Choo also said the appellants were charged based on an independent report by the Public Works Department (JKR), adding that the prosecution could have misapprehended the facts or misjudged the strength of the evidence, but that it could not be concluded that there was no probable or reasonable cause to prosecute the appellants.
He also said the High Court was correct to find that the appellants' action for false imprisonment has been time-barred.

The appellants - Razali Dollah, Zakaria Jusoh, Rahim Mohamad, Shariman Azam Shafie, Zamri Abdul Mana, Che Forzi Che Abd Che Abd Aziz, Abdul Rahim Awang, Mohamad Nizam Wahit, Enche Baharuddin Enche Endut, Salim Berahim, Ahmad Atma Ali@Yusof, Abdullah Embong, Othman Omar, Mohd Ramadhan Baharudin, Mohd Amir Ismadi Md Ghani, Mohd Zaid Ahmad@Mat, Mohamad Sari Ngah, Abdul Rashid Muda, Yusof Omar, Fakru Prazi Nordin and Shahairi Abd Wahab - were arrested by MACC for investigations relating to the alleged misappropriation of a fishermen housing repair project in 2014.
They were subsequently charged in the Kuala Terengganu Sessions Court and released on bail on Nov 17, 2014.

The trial was conducted, and on July 31, 2017, the Sessions Court discharged and acquitted them at the end of the prosecution's case. The prosecution filed an appeal but subsequently withdrew it on February 22, 2019.

Nearly seven years after their arrest, the appellants filed the civil suit naming five defendants, including the Attorney-General, MACC Chief Commissioner, MACC and the government of Malaysia and a MACC officer.
They sought, among others, general damages and aggravated damages of RM1 million for each of them and RM10 million in exemplary damages for all the appellants.
On May 8, this year, the Kuala Terengganu High Court dismissed the appellants' suit.

At the Court of Appeal proceeding today, Mohammad Rafaei Adnan and Alif Danial Ahmad Shahrulnizam represented the appellants while Senior Federal Counsel Liew Horng Bin and Federal Counsel Ahmad Faiz Abd Raoff appeared for the MACC and government.

5d77baf8f2f0dd15: Live action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucrat Every Friday night on a community sports field in Melbourne’s inner north, a few hundred nerds dress up in historical armour and attack each other with foam latex swords. It’s the biggest thing in my life outside of comedy, and the two scenes have a lot in common. Everyone’s broke. Everyone was bullied in high school. No one gets into Larp or standup if things are going well. Continue reading...
f945e72f077b5bc3: KUALA LUMPUR: True love is often said to be worth its weight in gold, but for newlyweds Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman and Bella Astillah, their fans have taken that sentiment quite literally.

Following the joyous celebration of their recent nuptials, the Muar Member of Parliament and the popular singer-actress were treated to a heartwarming double surprise courtesy of their dedicated fan club, Team Bass Official (TBO).

Beyond showering the couple with warm wishes, the devoted group of supporters marked the union by funding two deeply meaningful initiatives: a bespoke gold family heirloom and a charitable water well in West Africa.

Taking to social media, TBO revealed the touching story behind their choice of wedding present — a custom-crafted 999 fine gold bar intricately engraved with the portraits of Syed Saddiq, Bella, and her two children, Ayden Adrean, 7, and Ara Adreanna, 4.
The fan club shared that considerable thought went into selecting a present that transcended transient material gifts.
"We spent a long time thinking about what would truly be a meaningful present for YB and Bella. We wanted something that was not only beautiful, but could be kept and cherished forever," TBO posted.
Their search eventually led them to Goldfinch, a local jeweller that took on the ambitious task of producing the custom piece.
The elaborate process required the company's proprietor to travel abroad specifically to collect and oversee the custom engraving.
Explaining the symbolic gesture, TBO noted that gold was chosen for its timeless quality.

"We chose gold not for its price tag, but because we hope that, just like gold which retains its value over time, the love and affection within this little family will grow even more precious with the passage of years."

"We imagine that one day, when Ayden and Ara are older, they will look at this carving and know there was once a group of people, bound not by blood but by genuine affection, who rejoiced in their family's happiness," the group added.
A video circulating on social media captured the newlyweds' genuine awe and delight upon unboxing the shimmering keepsake during a recent celebration with their supporters.
TBO confirmed that the tribute was made possible through collective contributions from "BASSties" across diverse backgrounds.
The golden token follows another noble gesture orchestrated by TBO in conjunction with the wedding — the sponsorship of a water well for a village community in Guinea, Africa.

Organised with the assistance of local personality Fila Amir and her Guinean husband, Adama, the water project aims to provide clean, accessible water to villagers in need as a form of wakaf (endowment) in the couple's honour.
In a light-hearted post sharing footage from the remote village, TBO admitted to a humorous misunderstanding when reviewing the initial video sent from the site.

"When we received the clip, we asked Fila why the local lady in the video looked so cross with us," the fan club recounted with a laugh. "Fila reassured us, saying, 'Oh no, she isn't angry at all! She's offering a prayer of gratitude and expressing her heartfelt thanks to everyone who contributed to the well.'"
TBO teasingly apologised for the grainy footage — captured on a field worker's phone — promising to upload a full-length video of the project in due course.

Closing their tribute to the couple, the fan club offered a moving prayer for their future: "Receptions will end, flowers will wither, and guests will depart. But we hope these small memories endure for years to come. May Allah protect your love, bless your household, and shower your family of four with eternal happiness."
